name: Structured control flow
summary: if/else, while and for blocks with single entry/exit instead of arbitrary GOTO jumps.

origin.note: Formalised by Böhm–Jacopini (1966) and Dijkstra's 'Go To Statement Considered Harmful' (1968).

name: Lexical block scope
summary: Nested blocks introduce their own variables, visible only inside the block (lexical scoping).

name: Recursion
summary: Procedures that call themselves, supported by a call stack.

origin.note: ALGOL 60 brought recursive procedures to imperative languages.

name: Exception handling
summary: Non-local transfer of control for error conditions with handlers (try/catch, raise/rescue).

origin.note: PL/I ON-conditions; LISP 1.5 ERRORSET (1962) was an earlier error trap, and CLU (1975) introduced the structured signal/except model most languages follow.

name: Coroutines
summary: Routines that can suspend and resume, cooperatively passing control.

origin.note: Term coined by Melvin Conway in 1958.

name: Iterators & generators
summary: Functions that lazily yield a sequence of values (yield).

origin.note: CLU iterators (after Alphard's generators); Icon (1977) made any expression a generator driven by goal-directed backtracking, and PEP 255 cites Icon as a model for Python's.

name: Structural pattern matching
summary: Destructure data by shape and dispatch on it (match/case with bindings).

name: Proper tail calls
summary: Calls in tail position reuse the stack frame, so recursion can express unbounded loops.

name: First-class continuations
summary: Capture 'the rest of the computation' as a value (call/cc) to build any control structure.

origin.note: Anticipated by Landin's J operator (1965).

name: Static typing
summary: Types are checked at compile time.

origin.note: FORTRAN distinguished INTEGER and REAL (implicitly by first letter I–N).

name: Type inference
summary: The compiler deduces types without annotations (Hindley–Milner globally, or locally via var/auto/:=).

origin.note: Milner's algorithm W (1978).

name: Generics / parametric polymorphism
summary: Code parameterized over types (List<T>, templates, 'a list).

origin.note: CLU (1975) and Ada (1980) generics brought it to imperative languages.

name: Algebraic data types
summary: Sum types (tagged variants) and product types (records/tuples) as first-class type definitions.

origin.note: ALGOL 68 united modes (1968) were an earlier sum-type precursor; Hope combined sum types with pattern matching.

name: Type classes
summary: Ad-hoc polymorphism: types opt into interfaces via instances resolved by the type checker.

origin.note: Wadler & Blott, "How to make ad-hoc polymorphism less ad hoc" (proposed 1988, POPL 1989).

name: Option types / null safety
summary: Absence is modelled in the type (Option/Maybe/T?) so null dereferences are compile errors.

origin.note: LCF ML (1973) had sum types that could model absence; the named `option` type came with Standard ML. Contrast: the null reference Tony Hoare added to ALGOL W (1965), his "billion-dollar mistake".

name: Gradual typing
summary: Mix typed and untyped code in one program; annotations are optional and checked where present.

origin.note: Common Lisp type declarations were an early optional-typing precedent. Tobin-Hochstadt and Felleisen's 'Interlanguage migration' (DLS 2006) independently developed sound typed/untyped interoperation at module boundaries, shipped as Typed Scheme in PLT Scheme 4.0 (2008).

name: Structural typing
summary: Type compatibility is decided by shape (members) rather than by declared name.

origin.note: ALGOL 68 modes are equivalent by structure; Modula-3 (1988) revived structural equivalence, and Go and TypeScript made it mainstream.

name: Ownership & borrowing
summary: The type system tracks who owns memory and who may borrow it, giving memory safety without a GC.

origin.note: First described publicly in 2010 and refined 2012–2015; builds on region-based memory from Cyclone (2002) and linear/affine type theory.

name: Dependent types
summary: Types can depend on values (a vector of length n, a proof that i < n), so specifications and proofs are checked by the type checker.

origin.note: Automath was the first practical system to exploit the Curry–Howard correspondence; Martin-Löf type theory (1972) and the calculus of constructions (1988) followed, then Coq, Agda, Idris and Lean. Haskell (GADTs, DataKinds) and Scala (path-dependent types) offer restricted forms.

name: Interfaces / protocols
summary: Named sets of method signatures a type promises to implement, separate from inheritance.

origin.note: Objective-C protocols (NeXT); Java made interfaces mainstream.

name: Classes & objects
summary: Bundle state and behavior into objects instantiated from classes.

name: Inheritance
summary: Subclasses reuse and specialize the structure and behavior of superclasses.

name: Pure objects & message passing
summary: Every value is an object and all computation is sending messages, including control flow.

name: Prototype-based objects
summary: Objects inherit directly from other objects via delegation; no classes required.

name: Multiple dispatch
summary: The method chosen depends on the runtime types of all arguments, not just the receiver.

origin.note: CLOS generic functions.

name: Mixins & traits
summary: Compose reusable bundles of methods into classes without single-inheritance chains.

name: Abstract data types
summary: A type is defined by its operations while its representation is hidden (encapsulation).

origin.note: Barbara Liskov's CLU clusters; LCF ML's abstype was roughly contemporaneous.

name: Modules & separate compilation
summary: Programs split into modules with explicit export/import interfaces, compiled separately.

origin.note: Influenced by Xerox PARC's Mesa.

name: Design by contract
summary: Preconditions, postconditions and invariants as executable parts of the interface.

name: Operator overloading
summary: User-defined types can give their own meaning to operators like + and ==.

name: First-class functions & lambdas
summary: Functions are values: passed as arguments, returned, stored, and written anonymously.

origin.note: LAMBDA from Church's lambda calculus; MAPLIST as an early higher-order function.

name: Lexical closures
summary: Functions capture the variables of the scope they were defined in.

origin.note: Concept from Landin (1964); LISP 1.5 FUNARG (1962) was an early partial form, and Scheme made lexically scoped closures standard.

name: Immutable by default
summary: Bindings and data structures cannot be mutated unless explicitly opted in.

name: List comprehensions
summary: Set-builder notation for constructing collections: [x*x | x <- xs, even x].

name: Lazy evaluation
summary: Expressions are evaluated only when their value is needed, enabling infinite structures.

name: Purity & tracked effects
summary: Functions are pure by default; side effects are tracked in types (e.g. the IO monad).

origin.note: Monadic I/O arrived in Haskell 1.3 (1996).

name: Algebraic effect handlers
summary: User-defined effects that code can perform and handlers can intercept and resume.

origin.note: Plotkin and Pretnar's handlers of algebraic effects (2009), first built into a language in Eff; Frank (2017) typed them as abilities, which Unison adopted as its only effect mechanism.

name: Garbage collection
summary: The runtime automatically reclaims memory that is no longer reachable.

origin.note: Designed by John McCarthy for Lisp (1959); Daniel Edwards wrote the LISP 1.5 collector.

name: Automatic reference counting
summary: Objects are freed when their reference count drops to zero, deterministically.

name: Pointers & manual memory
summary: Explicit addresses, pointer arithmetic, and programmer-managed allocation and freeing.

origin.note: Harold Lawson is credited with the pointer variable for PL/I.

name: Actors & message passing
summary: Isolated share-nothing processes, each with private state and a mailbox, communicating only by asynchronous messages.

origin.note: Carl Hewitt's actor model (1973) is the theoretical root.

name: CSP channels
summary: Concurrent processes synchronise and communicate over typed channels.

origin.note: Tony Hoare's Communicating Sequential Processes (1978).

name: async / await
summary: Write asynchronous code in direct style; the compiler turns it into continuations or state machines (built on coroutine-style suspension).

origin.note: F# asynchronous workflows; C# 5 (2012) popularized the keywords.

name: Software transactional memory
summary: Shared-memory updates grouped into atomic transactions that retry on conflict.

origin.note: GHC's STM (Harris, Marlow, Peyton Jones, Herlihy).

name: Syntactic macros
summary: Code that transforms code at compile time, operating on syntax rather than text.

origin.note: Timothy Hart's MACRO definitions for Lisp 1.5.

name: Hygienic macros
summary: Macros that cannot accidentally capture or shadow identifiers at the use site.

origin.note: Kohlbecker et al.; standardized as syntax-rules in R4RS/R5RS.

name: Homoiconicity
summary: Programs are written in the language's own primary data structure (code is data).

name: Reflection
summary: Programs can inspect and modify their own structure (types, methods, classes) at runtime.

origin.note: Smalltalk made fully reflective object systems the norm.

name: Compile-time execution
summary: Ordinary code runs inside the compiler to compute values, types or generate code (CTFE, comptime).

origin.note: Lisp macros/eval-when; Zig's comptime unified it with normal code.

name: Hot code reloading
summary: Replace code in a running system without stopping it.

origin.note: The requirement came from Ericsson's telephone switches (PLEX/AXE); Smalltalk and Lisp images also allowed live redefinition.

name: Array programming
summary: Operations apply to whole arrays at once; loops disappear into vectorized primitives.

origin.note: Iverson's notation, published 1962.

name: Logic programming & unification
summary: Programs are facts and rules; execution is search via unification and backtracking.

name: Declarative queries
summary: Describe the result you want (relational algebra) and let the engine decide how to compute it.

name: Stack-based / concatenative
summary: Words operate on an implicit data stack; programs are compositions of words.

name: Significant indentation
summary: Indentation defines block structure (the off-side rule) instead of braces or keywords.

name: Built-in regular expressions
summary: Regular expressions for string matching: as literal syntax and operators (core) or via the standard library.

origin.note: SNOBOL (1962) pioneered string pattern matching but not regular expressions; AWK (1977) put /regex/ literals and the ~ match operator into a language's expressions, and Perl made regexes core syntax.
